maintopic: WESTERN GRAIN TRADE.
WESTERN GRAIN TRADE.
speechtext:
I wish to put on ' Hansard,' for the benefit of the Department of Trade and Commerce, a letter I received this morning. It is from Mr. R. McKenzie, secretary of the Grain Growers' Association of Manitoba, and is as follows:
Winnipeg, Can.,
April 28th, 1910.
Dr. Schaffner, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.
My dear sir,-
In further reference to the subject matter of my telegram to you, as you will no doubt know, the stock of the different grades in store in the terminal elevators was weighed in August of last year, and immediately on the close of navigation Inspector Gibbs made an estimate of the quantity in store of each grade by measurement. There is a report current that this estimate showed that the amount of high grade wheat shipped out far exceeded the amount received and as a consequence the Department of Trade and Commerce ordered the warehouse commissioner to institute an investigation. This investigation has been going on for some time and culminated in three of the terminal elevator companies being fined on information sworn out by Mr. Castle on the 22nd inst. Report has it that the solicitor representing the elevator company and the solicitor representing the department and Mr. Castle had arranged that the charge should be that of making false statements rather than the more serious charge of mixing grain. Be that report true or not, the fact remains that in place of the former being tried in open court, the solicitor for the terminal elevator companies met Mr. Daly in Mr. Hudson's office (Mr. Hudson being Mr. Castle's solicitor), and pleaded guilty, and was fined, the object apparently being to prevent the matter from coming before the public.
We think that this ' star chamber ' method of holding court should not be tolerated. If these terminal elevators are offenders against the law they should be treated as other offenders. It is a matter of common knowledge that practices in contravention of the law and against the best interests of the country were indulged in in these elevators for many years, and when the offenders were once brought to justice there should be no effort to endeavour to minimize the effect it would have. A simple fine is no punishment to these people. Publicity is what they are afraid of.
In the few days you have at your disposal before the House prorogues, will you, in the interests of the farmers, do what you can to get Mr. Castle's report and all correspondence brought down so that the public may know what has been done. I do not think at all that the Department of Trade and Commerce want to conceal anything, and there should be no disposition on the part of anyone to protect those who are accused of tampering with our grades. Our government undertakes to deliver our grain on the world's market according to specifications defined by statutes. Their inspectors compel the farmers to meet the requirements of the specifications and they should see that their inspectors should also compel those who handle our grain to comply with the require-

meats of those specifications in the handling of our grain.
Yours very truly,
r. McKenzie,
Secretary.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WESTERN GRAIN TRADE.
speechtext: Following up the subject which my hon. friend (Mr. Schaffner) has just laid before the House, I may say that Mr. Castle's report on this case was laid on the table on Friday.

speechtext:
I would like to read a report from the superintendent of immigration on the subject brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) some days ago:
With regard to the letter read in parliament on the 26th instant, by Mr. Lennox, M.P., I beg to state that full inquiry had been made into the question of the delay of passengers ex SS. ' Corsican ' before the matter was brought up in the House.
Under date of April 4, M. J. V. Lanta-lum, our agent at St. John, wrote giving his reasons for the action he took. According to his report the ' Corsican ' entered the dock at ten minutes to six o'clock, having on board 16 saloon, 364 2nd cabin and 250 steerage passengers. Mr. Lantalum's contention is that had the passengers been landed it would have been very late in the night before their baggage could be checked and passengers started on their railway journey. In support of his contention that it would be very late before the passengers would be able to get away from St. John, Mr. Lantalum mentions the fact that although landed at 9.05 a.m. Sunday morning, it was 3.30 in the afternoon before they got the first train away, and 4,15 when the second train left, seven hours and ten minutes from the time of landing until the last train left. Mr. Lantalum points out that if it required seven hours and ten minutes to check the luggage, &c,, during daylight on Sunday, it is only reasonable to suppose that it would have required a much longer time at night when the passengers were tired and other circumstances not so favourable. He also contends it would have been a hardship for the women and children to remain awake while the preparations were being made. It is evident there was a difference of opinion among the passengers as to what should be done, many being of the same opinion as Mr. Lennox's correspondent, that they were undergoing a hardship by being delayed. On the other hand Mr. Lantalum says in his report:
* Many of the passengers were very much pleased at being kept on the ship all night as they said they had a good night's rest which would enable them to stand the long rail journey. One head of a family thanked the immigration authorities warmly for it.'
It is quite evident that Mr. Lantalum's action was taken solely in the interests of the passengers, and while I personally think it would have been wiser to have landed them,
I do not think Mr. Lantalum is open to any censure for the action he took. I am, how-

speechtext: ever, notifying him in future that when boats whose passengers had been examined at Halifax reach St. John before 8 p.m., he is to allow them to land, providing the steamship and railway companies desire him to do so.

maintopic: DELAY IN MAILS BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LOWER PROVINCES.
DELAY IN MAILS BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LOWER PROVINCES.
speechtext: I would like to invite the attention of the Postmaster General to the subject of the transmission of mails from Ontario to points east of Montreal, particularly to the maritime provinces. Letters mailed in Toronto or at Ottawa, or at any other point in Ontario west of Montreal, in the evening of any day, reach, in the ordinary course, Montreal on the next morning. They are there held apparently until the evening of that day, and are then sent out in the Canadian Pacific railway mail train to points east. Apparently, the Post Office Department is not aware that there is a mail train leaving by the Intercolonial at 12 o'clock each day, and if these letters and other mail matter were transmitted by that Intercolonial train, they would reach Moncton and other points east much earlier, and reach the recipients fully a day in advance of the time when they actually reach their destination. The difficulty appears to be in connection with the transfer of mails at Montreal. It seems to me that the letters should be sent forward by the Intercolonial at 12 o'clock, instead of being held in Montreal until 7.25 the same day.

maintopic: DELAY IN MAILS BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LOWER PROVINCES.
speechtext: That would apply only to mail for the north shore counties in New Brunswick.

maintopic: DELAY IN MAILS BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LOWER PROVINCES.
speechtext:
The mails for Fredericton and St. John of course reach St. John
about the same time if they go by the Intercolonial. But the complaint arises in connection with the mails for Moncton, and points east on the Intercolonial in Nova Scotia and at other points in New Brunswick.

maintopic: DELAY IN MAILS BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LOWER PROVINCES.
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend has called my attention to that defect in the service. He saw me the other day, and immediately I wrote to the Montreal postal authorities to see that all mail destined to the lower provinces arriving in Montreal in the morning, should be forwarded by the noon train. There is no reason why the mails should not be transferred at once. A letter leaving Ottawa at night, even late at night, reaches Montreal at 8 o'clock in the morning by the western train. There is no reason why the mails should not be transferred from the Windsor station to the Grand Trunk station between 8 or 8.30 in the evening and 12 o'clock next day. There is something wrong in the service there, and I will give the necessary instructions that the complaint be remedied at once.

maintopic: DELAY IN MAILS BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LOWER PROVINCES.
speechtext: I hope the Postmaster General will not think of making the change in regard to all the portions of the maritime provinces. If the arrangement proposed by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) were adopted, it would cause a delay in the arrival of mail at. St. John and Fredericton which are served by the Canadian Pacific railway sooner than by the Intercolonial.

maintopic: FOREST RESERVE AT OKA RIVER.
FOREST RESERVE AT OKA RIVER.
speechtext: I wish to call the attention of the departments interested to a matter which I brought up earlier in the session; I refer to a petition that was sent by the people of the municipality of Oka river complaining that, owing to the fact that the forest reservation was immediately south of that municipality, the water backs up there and gradually overflows the lands, and prevents the farmers from putting in their crops in the vicinity of that reserve. I wrote to the Minister of the Interior asking favourable consideration of this matter, also to the Minister of Public Works and to the Prime Minister. I think it is only a moderate request on behalf of the people of that municipality that they should be aided in some way to build drains to take care of the water that overflows their land from the timber reserve.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: FOREST RESERVE AT OKA RIVER.
speechtext:
Speaking for the Department of the Interior which is responsible for the existence of the forest reserve, I do not understand that the existence of that reserve has any particular bearing on the undesirable presence of the water. It is because of the topographical condition, for

which the department is not responsible, and therefore it seems to me that the department or the government cannot be called upon to make good a damage which does not exist because of the action of the department or of the government; it is something for which no department of the government is responsible. While I am speaking on this subject, I may be permitted to say that I think the subject of drainage is one that is essentially a provincial matter; under these circumstances I do not think it would be right and proper that the federal government should undertake to do that which is essentially a provincial work.

maintopic: FOREST RESERVE AT OKA RIVER.
speechtext: How can the province drain through Dominion lands?

maintopic: FOREST RESERVE AT OKA RIVER.
speechtext: I realize that the minister is right in a great measure when he says that drainage is essentially a matter that appertains to the local provincial governments, but when they form a drainage district the lands within that district are charged with their share of the expense. It is impossible, as I understand, to charge Dominion lands and I just ask as a matter of fair play to the municipality that the Dominion contribute in some way towards the draining of this land which is absolutely necesary owing to the fact of the wooded country being immediately south of the municipality.

maintopic: FOREST RESERVE AT OKA RIVER.
speechtext:
I may say to the minister what my hon. friend contends for has been adopted by this House as a principle in regard to Dominion railways. The Dominion railways could not be made to contribute to the cost of draining their lands as well as the adjoining lands by provincial authority, but we saw the evil and we agreed to amend the Railway Act a few years ago by providing that we would make the Dominion railways which are under the control of this country contribute, under the provincial authority, in the same manner as my hon. friend contends that Dominion lands should.
I think that parliament, in order to be consistent, should adopt the same system of legislation as that which was adopted in regard to the Dominion railways and for the same reason that Dominion lands should contribute as contended for by my hon. friend.

speechtext:
House again in committee on Bill (No. 210) to incorporate the Retail Grocers' Association of Canada.-Mr. Gervais.
On section 1, incorporation:

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext:
I was unfortunately prevented from being in my seat on Friday evening when this Bill was under discussion, otherwise I would have taken occasion to express my judgment on it. It seems to me that this legislation properly belongs to the provincial legislatures, and that at this stage of the session certainly the time of this House should not be taken up with it. We have had similar legislation before parliament this very session. I understand this legislation is designed to protect the retail merchants in the several provinces. We have had legislation proposed with a view to protect the consumer, and that legislation met with but scant courtesy at the hands of parliament. This legislation, I am sure, is not any more entitled to consideration. I wish to be placed on record as entirely opposed to the measure in its general principles and also in detail. It is not necessary for these men to apply to this parliament for legislation to govern any association which they may have. While I can understand that there may be some reason for the wholesale merchants having Dominion incorporation, the same reasons do not apply in the case qf a retail merchant whose business horizon is necessarily a very narrow one, certainly not extending beyond his own province. Many of them do not go in their business transactions beyond the the community in which they reside. The retail merchants should go to their provincial legislatures for incorporation. It cannot be argued that the provinces have no jurisdiction over such matters. There is too strong a tendency for the Dominion to en-Mr. J. A. CURRIE.
croach on the provincial jurisdiction, and we should not permit these gentlemen to take up the time of this House. I feel that this committee should at this moment take a very determined stand against advancing this Bill any further during the present session at least.

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext: I had hoped the Prime Minister would be in his place when this Bill came up this morning, because I wanted to make an appeal to him, but as the Minister of Public Works is apparently leading the House in his absence, I would appeal to him. When the Bill first came up, a motion was made that the committee rise after the first section had been defeated by a considerable majority, but in deference to the feelings and wishes of the promoter that motion was withdrawn and the committee also consented to reconsider clause 1, the understanding of those who had voted against the Bill being that the promoter wished to withdraw it. This is the third time the Bill has been in the Committee o'f the Whole House. It took up the whole of the hour for private Bills on Friday- night. A large number of the members have gone away, as the session is drawing to a close and numbers of those who had voted against the Bill are not present. I appeal to the fairness of the promoter, and I ask the minister of Public Works if it is a fair proposition to press this Bill to a conclusion after we have had a division of the committee, now to bring it forward the third time, when a large number of the members are not here to vote.

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext: I might remind my hon. friend that this is a private Bill, and I do not think the government should be urged to take any charge of the committee upon it.

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext:
I am surprised to see this Bill again before the commitee. A few days ago we passed an Anti-Combine Bill. This morning, after discussing this three times, we are asked to pass a Bill that may lead to the formation of a huge combine. I cannot see where this Bill will help either the producer or the consumer, and I want to be placed on record as being straight against this Bill. I think it is unfair to bring it before the House at this time. The Bill was voted down and out the first time it was discussed, and now, when many members are away, it is brought forward again when we expect to prorogue in a short time.
Some hon MEMBERS. Vote.

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext:
Before the vote is taken I wish to say a few words. I have been listening to the so-called arguments

of the hon. gentlemen on three different occasions, on itwo nights and one day, and I think I am entitled to say a few words as a rejoinder of issue. The hon. gentlemen have tried to bring forward some arguments, tout I can assure you that nothing tout fiction, imagination, and something else which I shall not qualify has been advanced in support of the rejection of this Bill. Who are the promoters of this Bill? The retail merchants of Canada who are deserving so great consideration in Canada. I have been sitting in this House for seven years. In that time we have incorporated companies right and left at the request of groups of five persons. Provided five persons have paid $200, a fine of $100 sometimes, and sometimes a fee of $1,200, charters have been granted for the incorporation of companies of all kinds, so-called railway companies, so-called banking houses, so-called trade unions, so-called benevolent societies

as a matter of ract any group of five men in the land coming before this high court of parliament, the highest of Canada, has been granted a charter. Surely, before this parliament I can appeal under better circumstances than before any lower court, any Superior Court or Court of Appeal in my province and any group of men should be given a fair hearing in this parliament. In this particular case the retail merchants of our country should be granted a fair hearing, ^ as fair as the many hundreds of corporations that have ibeen created since confederation. I am now rather surprised to see so many hon. members of parliament speaking so lightly or slightingly of the retail merchants of Canada, the promoters of this Bill. As a matter of fact v'bo are the retail traders and wholesale traders of Canada? They are well known deserving and progressive people, they have done more for the benefit of Canada than most all of the workingmen of Canada.

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext: Yes, yes. That may be a surprise to you, but if you read the latest discoveries of social history you will find that the traders of the world have done an immense work for the progress and advancement of humanity. This has been the case in Canada and hon. members should not speak so disparagingly of the traders of Canada.

speechtext: What about the farmers?

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext:
The farmers have done their part of the work. What do you find in clause 1 of the Bill? That well known merchants all over Canada, numbering 272i
about 100, are now asking this parliament of Canada just to give them a charter to enable them to enjoy the powers and rights which are granted to any corporation under common law, under the civil law, under the law of confederation; because before all, I challenge any opponent of this Bill to point out to the House one paragraph, one sentence, one word, tending to show or of the nature to show that from the incorporation of this company a monopoly will toe created, or a so-called combine or that any illegal act will be committed, I repeat, it is fiction, it is imagination-I do not want to give out the third epithet-it is fiction and imagination to pretend that through the instrumentality of this Bill a monopoly will be created or a combine will be brought into existence. As I said, I am surprised to see how the retail merchants of Canada are being treated toy some hon. members of the House. The hon. member for Humboldt on Friday night last, tried but failed to advance reasons why we should not incorporate the Retail Merchants Association of Canada.
This House of parliament is a high court of justice to hear such demands as are made here and to grant them. Those demands or requests are framed in accordance with the constitution of 1867 and in accordance with the rules of parliamentary procedure. The Retail Merchants' Association of Canada have presented to this House a petition which has been properly signed. They have made the required deposit, given the necessary notice, and the Bill has been introduced in due form.

speechtext: There is no petitioner outside of Quebec and Ontario.

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext:
I beg the pardon of the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Em-merson). This incorporation is being sought for by the general traders of Canada. This Bill is not being forced upon this House by the association of retail merchants of but one province only. It has been presented in proper form with due notice; it has been reported to the House, which, I claim, is in duty bound to pass it. There is no reason for the rejection of the Bill. I challenge any lawyer in the House, and if the Minister of Justice were in his seat I would ask him to give his opinion, to say that he can find anything in the Bill which can be interpreted as trespassing upon or invading the rights of anybody or to show anything in the Bill which would create anything like a monopoly, combine or commercial company. The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) has told the House that the Retail Merchants' Association if incorporated would tend to create a monopoly or combine of

the nature which the House declined to accept in the Co-operative Societies Bill, If you read over the Bill relating to the so-called co-operative credit societies, you will find that the societies which sought to incorporate under that Act were asking powers to borrow money or to lend money. I was a little aggrieved to see so many members not of the legal profession putting a construction upon the Bill which cannot be justified by the general rules of interpretation. I call your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that there is no danger of any monopoly, trust or combine being created for the very simple reason that the association will have no power to buy goods or to sell goods or to borrow money. They will have no power to do any trade of any kind and they will be powerless to make any of the 20 contracts which are known under common law and under the civil law of the province of Quebec.

speechtext: What about section 6?

The limit is this, that they cannot use that money except for the purposes mentioned in section 2, and if any member will read over section 2 he will find that the association is powerless to make any contract or do any trade of any kind. My hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) is too clever a lawyer not to understand that under section 2 the association is powerless to make any contract, do any trade or any banking. He knows quite well that if they did, there are common law remedies, and the association could be brought to terms in any court of the land by a writ quo warranto on information. I repeat that this mischief feared by some hon. members is not possible under the provisions of the Bill, as the moment the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada tried to open a store, they could be enjoined by a writ quo warranto, while if they formed any combine they could be brought before the criminal courts and forced to account for their action. For, as we all know, there are provisions in the Criminal Code of Canada which have a very important bearing upon conspiracies in restraint of trade. Should any group of retail merchants use this association for the purpose of making what is known as a combine or monopoly, anybody in the land-anybody Mr. GERVAIS '
-can bring those offenders before the criminal courts. All fears of combine or monopoly through such a measure as this fade away the moment I draw attention to the fact that anybody in Canada may become informer and bring before the criminal court, not merely one man, but even all the members of this Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, to force them to withdraw from an illegal combine should any such be formed.
Then, there is a third remedy, and a very good one. Should the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada form a combine, the law which has just been enacted at the instance of the Minister of Labour can be made use of to prevent the continuance of any such anti-commercial organization. Thus, we have the three remedies, legal and complete remedies, should this Act of Incorporation be taken advantage of for the purpose of forming a combine in restraint of trade: first, idle quo warranto on information of the Crown; second, the anticombines law; and, third, bringing before the criminal courts the merchants accused of maintaining a combine.
Some hon. members of this House call for the rejection of this Bill but without showing any reason for such a course. I have said, and I think I have shown, that the retail merchants of Canada are entitled to some little consideration from this House. And all they ask is the same consideration that is given to any group of five men, which groups have been incorporated right and left by this parliament, the only conditions demanded being, proper notice for one month, a deposit of $200, and the following of a procedure established under certain rules. The Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, are, purely and simply -yes, and I say exclusively-requesting this House to give them a charter of incorporation. Is there any good reason to dismiss such an application? I wonder if the opposition to this Bill can arise because two Bills relating to the incorporation of co-operative societies which have claimed the attention of the House for the last two sessions have been dismissed ? But it is rather queer to note that the most rabid opponents of the. Bill.now before us, who oppose it on the ground that its promoters have been fighting the co-operative Bills, never attended the sittings of the Banking and Commerce Committee before which the arguments for and against the co-operative Bills were brought out. My reason for suggesting this is that -western Ontario and in the Niagara peninsula we have two transmission companies in operation and another will be in operation in a very few -day-s, I expect. They transmit from the source of supply to large centres like Toronto, Hamilton and other places, tout they decline to consider the applications of people who wish to use their power in the intermediate territory. The people of the intermediate territory have to submit to -all the inconveniences and dangers of the transmission lines passing -their places, sometimes on the roadway, at all events crossing the roadway in many places, and in quite a number of places in front of their doors or between their doors -and the street or highway. It is only fair that if they have imposed upon them all the dangers and inconveniences they should be entitled to the benefits and conveniences that accrue to the central points. In the case of this particular company it will be very much more advantageous, if, betvreen Ottawa and Montreal there should spring up a hundred towns where manufacturing industries will be established, where workmen can live in comfort and with healthy surroundings free from the disadvantages which generally afflict the congested communities in the great -cities, than it would be to have this power transmitted In 'bulk to Montreal, there to develop that city's industries and increase its population by 100,000. centralization of population from the great cities could be effected to a wonderful degree by these transmission lines. These transmission lines may be useful in building up .thriving communities throughout the country without continuing to further stimulate the centralization of everything around large cities. maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext:
I want to put myself briefly on record with regard to this Bill.
I think this Bill should never have come before parliament at all. It is absolutely unconstitutional, it is confiscatory, it puts back civilization hundreds of years. It means that because a few stockholders in a railway company do not want to sell their stock* to the city of Guelph which owns the rest of the stock of the railway, the city asks this parliament to direct them by force to sell the city the stock at a certain price, namely, $400 a share. I say we have no business to put ourselves in the position of interfering with such a matter at all. It is not like a matter of expropriation where a man's land can be taken to build a railroad. The city of Guelph can control this road, these are a minority of the stockholders. It is said on the one hand that they are trustees for the city of Guelph, and should hand over their stock; on the other hand it is said that they are not trustees, and the preamble of the Bill alleges that they are agents, which fact is disputed. And instead of the city going to the courts to get a declaration as to whether these men are agents and thereby bound to transfer that stock, or as to whether they are not, we are asked, in this twentieth century, to do what we should never have been asked to do, the suggestion should never have been made, and I cannot imagine that the people who are bringing this Bill forward really understand what it is they are asking us to do. The city of Guelph has a railway. It practically owns it all with the exception of a very few shares. There are some four of five other shareholders. It has turned out a good thing for the pro-



moters. These people have an investment that is worth a great premium to them. It happens that it has 'been a profitable investment or speculation. Suppose the converse were the case. If, as in many cases in this country, since we started to build railways, people bad put their money into a railway and lost it, if the enterprise had been an absolute failure, could they come and ask the municipality which was going to get the .benefit out of it, to take it off their hands, pay them a certain price for it and ask this parliament to fix that price? That is exactly what we are asked to do by this Bill. My first reason for opposing it is that we are not competent, to judge the merits of this matter, if there are any merits to be decided as to whether these people are trustees or agents, and therefore in equity should hand over their stock

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext: What interest have they in it?

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext: There are three or four of them who each own a share.

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext: What is a share worth?

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext: They paid $100 each for them and the city of Guelph says: We will give you $100 and 6 per cent compounded, making a total of $400 for each share if you will sell us your stock. Parliament is asked to declare that these people must do so; first, that without their consent they must sell their stock, and secondly, that we shall fix the price of these shares. I ask hon. gentlemen.if we are competent to decide any question that we are asked arbitrarily to act upon in regard. to it. If these people are trustees or agents the courts of the land can so declare. It is fair to say so as not to mislead any gentleman in this House, that it was admitted by the promoters of this Bill that technically these people were not trustees and that there is an obstacle in the way of the courts so declaring. Where are we going to stop if we begin this thing? If you grant that a man is not a trustee, that you cannot succeed in court in proving that he is, that he is not obliged to transfer his stock to you, are we to be told by the city of Guelph or by some other municipality that because the city wants this .to be done this House must enact that the property of this man must be expropriated. It means confiscation. Take the case where a man would go out and grub stake people, supply money and try to develop a coal mine. Suppose that he spends a thousand dollars in prospecting each mine, and one mine near a town or city which wants the coal turns out to be a .paying concern. According to Uiis Bill which we are asked to pass, in principle, we will be compelled to

maintopic: COAL SUPPLY FOR NOVA SCOTIA LIGHTHOUSE KEEPERS.
speechtext:
say: The public interest requires that you shall turn that coal mine over to the city. You have spent a lot of money in other parts of the country on what never turned out to be paying concerns, but this property has turned out well and we will give you what it has cost you to locate and develop it and 6 per cent interest compounded, and you must turn it over .to the city which is nearest you and which wants that coal. I say that is confiscation. I say it is not civilization. This is not civilized legislation or legislation that is in accordance with British institutions or principles. If we open the door I do not know where it will end. I want to be quite understood as not _ .saying that I think this is not a fair price. I am not competent to judge whether it is a fair price or not. I am not saying that I think they should have more, and I am not saying that they were the agents or trustees of the city of Guelph, and that the city .should not pay them anything. I am not competent to judge that, and I do not think that there is .any legal gentleman in this House who will say that he is. The courts of the land are there to say whether they are trustees. The city of Guelph can give evidence to show that they are and they can get the courts to issue a mandamus compelling this transfer without coming to parliament. Surely, it is a most unheard of proposition that this parliament must put itself in the position of saying, in the most socialistic way, that it shall determine what a certain " man's property is worth, which he is not obliged to sell by the laws of the land, and that it shall .so determine upon evidence, such as we have brought before us, which would not be admissable in a court of law. We are asked to say that if a man is getting a fair price for something that he owns, which he has acquired, which he has a Tight to speculate in if he wants to, he must transfer it, _ not for the .public service of the Dominion, but for the benefit of a municipality. 2.	Our treaty with France does not entitle us to the French minimum tariff on everything, neither does France receive our intermediate tariff on everything. We are entitled to the French minimum tariff on a list of articles which practically covers everything of importance that Canada has been exporting. On all these products we continue to receive the mostfavoured-nation treatment and the United States receives no advantage over us.
There are no available public documents setting forth the exact arrangement recently made between France and the United States. But press statements informally issued by the United States State Department are to the effect that France, to obtain the American minimum tariff, granted the French minimum rates on products covering 96 per cent,of the United States exports to France. Canada to obtain the same consideration from the United States made a reduction in her general tariff on articles representing less than three per cent of American exports to Canada.
3.	The German government grants to
the countries named the full conventional tariff in return for the granting by those countries of their lowest tariff rate to foreign countries.	.
Canada does not grant to Germany the lowest rates which are granted to other foreign countries, and consequently cannot claim the full German conventional tariff. But Canada receives from Germany the conventional tariff on a list of articles which it is believed, cover all the important articles of Canadian export.

1.	How many meetings of Select Standing Committees and Special Committees have been held during the present session of parliament?
2.	Has it been found necessary to employ outside assistance to take the notes of evidence in any of the committees? If so, why?
3.	In how many committees, and how often, has an extra staff of stenographers been required, and what has been the total cost of such assistance?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
1.	The number of meetings of select standing committees during the present session, up to April 30, has been 141; special committees 122.
2.	It has been necessary to employ outside assistance to take the notes of evidence in some of the committees.
The necessity arose by reason of the fact that more- than two of the committees were sitting at the same time, and consequently the present staff of two reporters was unable to keep up with the work.
3.	Extra stenographers have been employed in connection with eight different committees and at 76 meetings of the same.
The amount paid for such assistance to date is $2,549.83, and there remains unpaid about $400.

Western Canada, a greater field has been opened up by reason of the Western Associated Press taking the full Canadian Associated Press services and through its membership, distributing the news to some fifteen papers located between Winnipeg and Vancouver, so that the people of the west have now the advantage of reading empire news from a British source-a complete and impartial service furnished by news gatherers who know the wants of the Canadian reading public.
The Works of the Past Tiro Years.
Permit me to call your attention to the extensive news field that has been covered by the association. It has handled trade, market, cattle and produce reports which have earned for it the commendation of the classes of men directly interested in the trade, as well as of retail men who are served by the wholesalers.
Further, we cover all news appearing in the British press affecting any of the colonies, every discussion in the British parliament on Canadian affairs, the opinions of the British press on colonial subjects and reports of all Canadian cases coming before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and its decisions. These have all been promptly cabled to Canada. The important matter of the Canadian cattle embargo received special attention during the discussions in the British parliament.
As one example of the good work done in Privy Council cases, it gave a great deal of satisfaction to the Canadian press and people that the Dominion Steel judgment which was of vital interest to the Canadian commercial world, was cabled almost in full by our service.
Other features of our service are also worthy of note.
The visits of our Canadian ministers in England in matters of business connected with Canada, have been chronicled, and when news offered it has been cabled. Negotiations in support of cable and postal reductions were also specially followed. Cables covering the successful visit of the Finance Minister in placing Canadian loans on the London market and his visit to France, and the resultant Frau co-Canadian Treaty, with the press and ministerial opinions, were covered at considerable length. Not only has Canadian news orginating in England been dealt with, but Australian, New Zealand and South African news items, such as parliamentary debates and press comments on general colonial subjects connected with tariffs and other imperial affairs. The proceedings of the Imperial Press Conference in London were cabled in extenso and the views on imperial matters of the visiting colonials were recorded at a cost of about $1,200. The Imperial Defence Conference also received due attention at a cost of about $800.
The recent British elections were covered in a manner never before attempted by a cable service. The press of Canada has paid the highest compliment to the Canadian Associated Press for the complete manner in which the returns of the British elections were given to

the Canadian people. The importance of the recent elections to Canada and the empire, fully merited the cost incurred. The service was simply perfect. It is worthy of remark that in the cabling of these returns the names of each parliamentary constituency and the contesting candidates and the number of votes polled by each candidate, were cabled. Further, condensations of all the speeches by both party leaders were sent daily during the progress of events. On this important subject the Canadian Associated Press gave about 30,000 words at a cost of $3,000. There were about 1,500 despatches, all of which were received without an error.
The West Indies Commission was also dealt with in a satisfactory manner, reports of the proceedings being sent daily from London. The German-Canadian Treaty was also covered with the British and German press views from day to day.
British parliamentary debates in the prepresent parliamentary crisis are also being furnished daily while press comments on the situation are given by our service, which is practically the only service on this continent keeping fully in touch with the British political situation.
In the realm of sport the Canadian Associated Press furnishes an efficient service. Such sporting events of national interest as the Olympic games were cabled fully and to the great satisfaction of the Canadian public. Football, cricket and such leading athletic events have also been cabled promptly. This service includes recording the result of all important races run in Great Britain.
The annual Bisley report is one of the features of the Canadian Associated Press service. This important national meeting is covered in a manner most gratifying to the Canadian public, and at considerable cost. The Canadian Associated Press is the only cable service covering the complete scores at Bisley.
Our service has been free of criticism during the last two years. Its cables are carefully edited and its London office uses excellent judgment in the selection of news to be forwarded. The members of the association have in their newspapers and in personal letters to the president, congratulated the management on the excellence of the services furnished.
There is one important point in connection with the Canadian Associated Press service which I desire to emphasize in this letter. It is this-our service practically goes to about thirty papers in Canada, that is, fifteen who are members of the association and about fifteen who are served by the Western Associated Press.
All these papers received the despatches daily. But there are a large number of dailies that do not take our service, but who use our despatches after our publication-not only dailies but a large number of weeklies. Some time ago an examination of the daily and weekly papers received in the head office at Toronto, revealed the fact that no less than sixty dailies and two hundred and fifty weeklies, non-members, were using the despatches of the Canadian Associated Press. Many of these dailies are not financially able to pay for the service. The point is that the Canadian Associated Press service has a much greater constituency outside of its membership Mr. FIELDING.
than it has within, so that indirectly the association serves a large proportion of the daily and weekly press of the Dominion, in fact, it reaches nearly all the newspaper readers of the Dominion.
The present income from membership and aid from the government is only sufficient to provide a daily average cable service of about 570 words.
To have a more extended service, that is, a general news service which would cover the same field as the American Associated Press, would involve three or four times the expenditure.
This suggested service could not be entertained while cable rates for press messages are at 10 cents a word. But, if the day ever arrives when the cable rate will be cut to six cents a word or less, a fairly good general service could be maintained for about double the present expenditure. The service would be a handpicked one which would give the largest amount of value for the verbiage received. In fact, by a close skeletonizing of the despatches, a good general service could be guaranteed. I merely mention the foregoing to show the possibilities of future service.
The present subsidy of $12,000 a year is for two years, expiring as before stated, on 30th June, 1910.
The association asks that the subsidy be lenewed for five years instead of two. The difficulty is that for a short period there is an uncertainty in the basis of rates we are able to quote. The withdrawal of government aid would make cable news a nonopoly of the richer members of the association and crowd out the smaller newspapers. The grant for two years does not give the necessary stability to our financial arrangements, and this prevents us attracting new members by offering them rates based on the certainty of a government grant for five years. In this event our income would be more settled. The smaller papers could be assured of a continued cable service and thus be delivered from the fear of being driven out by a greatly increased assessment.
I might point out that as a result of the government grant the farmers of this country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, are served with the latest prices as to cattle, cheese, butter, bacon and other such commodities, including a weekly * return of the hogs killed in Denmark and Ireland, which latter information is important to bacon producers of this country-so that virtually every newspaper reader in Canada is supplied with market reports that would never reach him if the government grant were withdrawn and cable news became the monopoly of a few papers rich enough to stand the heavy expense.
The government grant has enabled the [DOT] Canadian Associated Press to create a national news service. Its enterprises during the recent British elections enabled newspaper readers of Canada to know how the political fight was going from day to day. Had they had to depend on the American news service, which cares nothing about British elections or the variety of news interesting and valuable to Canada, their information would have been meagre.
In obedience to the instructions of the as-

sociation, I have submitted a set of facts which the association offers as ample justification of its request for a continuance of tfte government grant for the next five years.
If you require further information, the association will be glad to furnish such, either in the form of a letter or at an interview if you should grant us an opportunity of presenting our case verbally.
Your truly,
. J. ROSS ROBERTSON, President Canadian Associated Press.

Mr. FIELDING moved that the House go into committee to consider a certain proposed resolution respecting subsidies to dry-docks. He said:	There are several
dry-docks in Canada which have been built and owned by the Canadian government. They are not in any way affected by the resolutions which are now in your hands. There are other dry-docks which have been built by private corporations with the assistance of government subsidies. We have had on our statute-book for some years legislation designed to encourage the building of dry-docks and several docks have been so built. The law has been changed from time to time to meet the changing conditions of the country. As it 3tands now, the Governor in Council is authorized to grant a subsidy of three per cent per annum for a period of twenty years for the construction of an approved dry-dock not exceeding in cost $1,500,000. With the ever-increasing size of steamships, larger docks become necessary, and the need of these docks is emphasized at present in connection with the naval movement. Of course, it is recognized that new dry-docks are necessary for the ships of our own navy and for receiving and repairing any ships of the British navy which may be employed Mr. FIELDING.
on our coasts. We propose to readjust our dry-dock legislation and make it conform to modern requirements. We propose to divide our dry-docks into three classes. One which, for convenience, is called the third class is recognized by the terms of the existing law', that is, for what may be called a smaller or moderate size dock, we retain the present arrangement of a subsidy for twenty years of three per cent with a maximum cost of $1,500,000. Then, we have a larger size, called a second-class dock. In that case, the subsidy is for a period of twenty-five years, and the rate of interest three and a half per cent instead of three per cent, and the maximum cost $2,500,000. Then, we have a larger class, which we call a first-class dock for general and naval purposes. In that case, we still retain the rate of three and half per cent, but provide that it shall be for a period of thirty-five years, and that the maximum shall be $4,000,000. This first-class dock for general and naval purposes, we provide, must be at the making of any contract under this Act, capable of receiving for purposes of repair the largest ship in the British navy, and, necessarily, as that will involve a very large outlay, we have thought it well to be generous and liberal wdth our subsidy.

Not always. But the hon. member will see that under these resolutions we make alternative provision for fixed or floating docks. In the case of a floating dock, you can receive a vessel much longer than the dock itself, but you cannot do the same in a fixed dock. But I am told that the existing dock in Halifax will take any ship in the Canadian trade, and, indeed, I believe it will take in what is ordinarily called a Dreadnought. But they are building a larger class of ship, called, I believe, for want of a better name, super-Dreadnought, and I believe that, neither the Halifax dock nor any other dock in Canada could receive such a vessel There are rival views as to the usefulness of the fixed or masonry dock and the float ing dock. It is one of these questions on which engineers have different opinions. Perhaps the proper view is that in some localities the masonry dock is best while other localities can be served by the floating dock which will cost less money. In the resolution we are making provision for either as may be deemed best. Then, we are making provision for the enlargement of any * existing dock, so that, if the pro-

prietors of any present dock wish to avail themselves of this present subsidy and provide a larger dock the scheme will admit of their doing so. What we provide for in that case is that we may take the value of any existing dock, so far as it is useful for the purpose of enlargement, and include it in the cost of the new undertaking under which the subsidy provided by these resolutions may be paid. But as these docks have already received subsidies, we provide that what they have received shall be deducted, so that the effect will be that an existing dock may be rebuilt under the new scheme, but deducting any subsidies already paid. I think it will be found that this is a fair and reasonable arrangement. The matter is one of considerable detail, but I think I have said all that is necessary to indicate the general character of the proposed scheme.

! The floating dock is all right enough for * the purpose of repairs, but the hon. gentleman must know that a dry-dock is now used for more purposes than the mere repairing of a ship. In fact, owing to the [DOT] change in the character of the docks in the United States, with the exception of two or three old ones on the Atlantic coast, ships are now built at the slips at the sides of the docks, and they are launched sideways. It is only at a few places in the old country, and at one or two places on the Atlantic coast in the United States that they continue to launch ships endways. To give the House an idea of the advantage of building a ship alongside of the dry-dock, I may say that when a ship is built to be launched by the stern or the head, in every measurement that is taken on that vessel from the plumb line, there has to be an allowance made. The doors have all to be hung on a slant, while when a ship is built alongside of the dry-dock and dropped in squarley, it is possible to plumb and true up everything about it by gravity. These are modern conditions, and for that reason I say that when this government are paying out money for dry-docks, it must be prepared to have modern slips such as they have in Germany and the United States, where they can build warships if they want to at the side of the dock and launch them into the dock sideways. The plant that has to be used at a dry-dock is the same as that used foi* ship-building. There is no need of having two yards, because the one can be used for two purposes. If you are going to establish a dry-dock in a barbarous country or far away from civilization and mechanics such as in Manila or the Bermudas or at a point from which you may expect to move it again and take it to some other place, then, of course, the floating dry-dock is the proper thing to have. It would be a good plan no doubt to have a floating dry dock or two so that you could haul them aTound amongst the doubtful constituencies at election time. But, as far as the actual work of a dry-dock is concerned it should be at a fyted place where the cars could go alongside with material. Material now is very heavy and there must be an opportunity for taking the cars alongside of the dock.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: What proportion of this amount is traceable to the establishment of a Canadian navy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
I think that the larger dock or what I might call the first-class dock may be regarded as being attributable in some degree to the naval movement. The construction of a large dry-dock suitable for the largest vessels of the British navy would be regarded as desirable no doubt from the point of view of the naval question. While I do not sav that we would not have desired such a large dock without it, I do say that the naval movement has given additional reason why we should have large docks.
Mr. BOYCE I would like to ask the minister how this enactment will apply to applications for subsidies under the old regulations?

maintopic: QUESTIONS.

speechtext: The second class?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.

The second class is a new class. A new application may be made, or if the dock has been constructed of a smaller class and they wish to enlarge it we will have power under this Act to permit them to do so.
Mr. BOYCE Assuming that the plans and specifications and all the obligations under the old law are complied with and the dock conforms to the second class, would that application be dealt \vith as an application for a subsidy under this or under the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: About a year ago an application was made for a dry-dock subsidy, and the town of Sault Ste. Marie has passed a by-law granting certain aid. I understand that all the details under the old Act have been complied with. Are they entitled to the increased subsidy?

maintopic: QUESTIONS.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.

speechtext: Can tht government authorize an unlimited number of docks under this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: They could do so at any time for the last 25 years.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: What expert advice has the government had on the important question of properly framing these conditions set out in clauses 1, 2 and 3?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: We naturally turned to the engineers of the Public Works Department, and to some extent of the Marine Department, and we have had occasion to make some inquiry of the admiralty. From these various sources we have been able to define the details.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
The Minister of Public Works with some gusto stated that the plans for the Sault Ste. Marie dry-dock had not yet been approved by the department.
I have several times asked in the House as to this matter, and it was always going to be attended to. Will the minister let us know now' what the difficulty is. At the same time, and through the same solicitor a similar application was made for a subsidy by a Port Arthur firm which the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Conmee) was advocating, and the Minister of Public Works went up to turn the first sod of that dock. Marie dry-dock, and in favour of the Port Arthur dry-dock by reason of certain political influences. _ There does seem to be a grain of truth in this. Will the minister explain if he can why the Sault Ste. Marie dry-dock specifications have not been approved w'hile the Port Arthur dry-dock, the application for which was made at the same time, has

maintopic: QUESTIONS.

It is reported generally, and it has been conveyed to me as gossip and rumour.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. My hon. friend should not take street gossip as the foundation for assertions in this House. Any delay which has occurred is a result of the action of^ the company itself. The company submitted certain plans and specifications, and they afterwards desired I should not act upon these plans, because they wished to make an alteration, and that alteration has not yet been submitted to me for consideration.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: CLtEBIE. Is it the policy of the government to decide where a dry-dock will be established, and where there is necessity for it, or are these docks to be erected in any old place at all where some Tom, Dick or Harry, may want to establish one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
The location has to be approved by the government on the report

of the Minister of Public Works. Any body has the right to go into the construction of a dry-dock, but he cannot get a subsidy until he has had the application approved and entered into the contract.

speechtext:
House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
1.	Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the Minister of Finance be authorized to pay out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada, for the purposes hereinafter referred to, in addition to the sums authorized to be paid under the provisions of chapter 10 of the Acts of 1899, an Act respecting the city of Ottawa, and amending Act, chapter 45 of the Acts of 1903, the sum of forty thousand dollars annually, for a period of ten years from the first day of July, 1909, making a total annual payment during said period of one hundred thousand dollars; such additional sums to be paid into a chartered bank to be designated by the minister, to the credit of the Ottawa Improvement Commission, and to be by the commission expended for all or any of the purposes for which the commission is authorized by section 7 of said chapter 10, to expend sums placed at its credit.
2.	That the Minister of Finance be authorized to pay out of the consolidated revenue fund to the corporation of the city of Ottawa, as a contribution to the maintenance of the fire protection service of the corporation, the sum of fifteen "thousand dollars annually for a period of ten years from the first day of July, 1909, the first of such payments to be made as soon as may be after the passing of any Act founded on these resolutions, and the remaining nine annual payments to be payable in advance during the month of July in each year, the last payment to be made in the month of July, 1918.-Mr. Fielding.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
It will be remembered that a few years ago parliament took the view that the national capital of Canada had a special claim upon us for consideration, and that not merely for the pleasing of the citizens of Ottawa, but as a matter of pride in the national capital, the government should contribute an annual sum for the improvement of the city. A body known as the Ottawa Improvement Commission was appointed 'and the government granted the sum of $60,000 per annum to the city of Ottawa, or rather to the Ottawa Improvement Commission. Arrangements were made whereby the city of Ottawa was represented on the commission, but the control was largely in the hands of the government through its
commissioners. The commission did very excellent work, and I think it will be admitted that within the space of a very few years a great improvement has been made. I think the success of the commission in beautifying the national capital has probably commended their work to the consideration of the House, and will render the House well disposed towards the extension of the aid which it is now proposed to grant. The sum we have hitherto granted is $60,000 per annum. It is only fair to say that in reality that was an additional grant of $45,000, because _prior to that time we had been .paying $15,000 to the city for fire protection and water. It is proposed now, in addition to the $60,000 which we have been paying.them, to add a sum of $40,000, making a grant of $100,000 per annum to be paid to the commission, and we also propose to pay the city $15,000 as we paid in former years for the fire and water service. The arrangements of the past have been pretty well understood. The operations, I think, have, on the whole, proved satisfactory and I am hopeful that the proposal to give this further aid for the beautifying of the national capital, will commend itself to the judgment of the House.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I have no desire to offer any opposition, but in the city of Halifax we have a large amount of Dominion government property, somewhere between $5,000,000 and $8,000,000 worth, and I think it would be nothing but fair under the conditions that a grant of some kind should be made to the city of Halifax in connection with the keeping up and improving of streets there, the police, fire protection, and services of that kind. The Finance Minister is aware that a great portion of our very best water front is taken up now by the Dominion government and is exempt from taxation. This property was formerly owned by the imperial government, but it has now been handed over to the Canadian government, and I really think Halifax is entitled to some consideration on that account. The Finance Minister, knowing the situation as well as I do, will certainly sympathize with that request. We have a large street mileage, and do a great deal to keep up the streets, 'sidewalks, etc., and everything of tlhat kind is done without assistance from the government, as they are exempt from taxation of all kinds, even for fire purposes. The city is well governed, and well prepared to give every accommodation to people there and this government should certainly give some assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
An appeal for the city of Halifax naturally enlists my sympathy. We are doing this for Ottawa not merely to please our good friends the citizens of

Ottawa but because Ottawa is our national capital. Once we depart from that principle and grant assistance to Halifax then a dozen other cities will claim like assistance.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: There is no other like Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: To use a slang expression, there are others; it is not the only pebble on the beach. We can justify to a moderate extent a generous grant for the beautifying of the national capital because it is the capital, but once we get away from that principle and undertake to deal with other cities my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) will discover that he has a claim for some city up in his constituency which he would assure us was as important as Halifax. Of course he would be wrong, but he would urge it. I do not want to express any opinion that would govern us in the future, but so far as I can see the reason we give for a grant to Ottawa would not apply to any other city in the Dominion. It is because Ottawa is the capital that we give the grant. Just at present Halifax is not the capital-it may become so at some future time.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I have never asked for any favour for my county, but the argument advanced for an expenditure of money here is not alone that it is the capital but because the civil service and the government buildings and many government institutions and persons are exempt from taxation here and the city has to maintain the usual civic services. If the government has property in Halifax which is a burden to the taxpayers in that city and does not contribute any taxation, the electors of Victoria and Haliburton will be only too ready to say that the government should do something as an equivalent to their taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: We have it in all parts of Canada.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman tell me another city in Canada, outside of Ottawa, that has $8,000,000 worth of government property? Will he name one with $4,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend will not claim that Halifax has too much Dominion property. I have sometimes tried to get more for it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman did not do it, it was imperial property and the imperial government handed it over. If this government had to purchase it I am inclined to think we would not have got so much. The hon. gentleman has said that there are other cities that have the same claim.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I said they would urge that they had.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
That is a mistake. I ask him to name another city that has $4,000,000 worth. This government did not pay for the property I spoke of. We have an armoury there that cost $300,000 to $400,000. It was not constructed by this government. I do not know anything that was built by them, except one elevator, towards which we had to contribute $55,-
000.	The city had to come up here and offer $55,000 before they could get the government to stir the Conservative government. They gave us an elevator, but that grain elevator was burned down and the present government offered to put up another one for $55,000. It might as well not have been built for it has never been much good to us. In fact I intended to ask the government to give us back our $55,000 because they got it under false pretences. It was understood that the railway company was going to put a terminus there but they have not done so. If there are any other cities in the Dominion that have the same claim, as Halifax, I am sure the people of Halifax will be delighted to contribute as they have contributed in the past to other enterprises in Canada. We do not come here begging for anything. My hon. friend, the Finance Minister, said there were hundreds of other cities who have got as much right to consideration as Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I said they think they have, not that they had.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I am not asking what other cities think, I am asking the Finance Minister if he thinks that we have a claim to some consideration or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I think this is a good Bill.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Yes, it is a good Bill to build up Ottawa. You started with $60,000, and goodness knows where you are going to stop. Next year you may be asking for $200,000. I am not complaining of Ottawa getting anything. It seems to be getting everything, and in a short time there will be no other place except Ottawa where we will be-able to spend a cent. I claim that Halifax is entitled to some consideration. The property is there, we give you every convenience, we have a well governed city, and we invite any of you to come down there and see us. We would like to see the Prime Minister there. The people would be very kind to Ijim if he came, notwithstanding^ that on many things they might not agree with him. But they are a kind hearted people and will give him a good reception. We also give you good streets, good sidewalks, a good police force, every thing in fact that we can have in a well governed city.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Everything good except the representation.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Now, if my hon. friend the Prime Minister thinks this claim is not good representation, I will tell the people when I go back what he says, and I am afraid his reception will not be quite so good as if he had never said it. I hope I am making a fair claim, and that if the Minister of Finance is not in sympathy with it, that the Prime Minister will be, because he has been in Halifax many times, and I hope he will be there again.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I could describe the property, but I do not want to take up the time of the House. I could show you that we have a property worth over $8,000,000, and, therefore, I think we are entitled to some consideration.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I would like to call the attention of the Finance Minister to a certain circumstance which has come under my observation. I presume this grant includes the driveway east of Rockcliffe and extending in the direction of the rifle range, does it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Yes, that is part of the work.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Well, I have observed that there is a retaining wall some little distance beyond Rockcliffe, and that it has been built of wood, a good deal of which is decayed. Now, it does not seem to me that that is a judicious expenditure of money. Stone is in abundance down there, and I think that when work of that kind is being executed it ought to be executed in a permanent way so that it will not require to be rebuilt in a short time. Building with wood is in itself a pretty expensive matter. I have noticed that several of the logs used in building the wall are partly decayed, and they must have been in that condition when they were put in.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Was that wood put in by the commission?

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: The walls would be built, I presume, by 'the Improvement Commission.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I do not think so.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I am referring to the driveway extending along the shore to the rifle Tanges. Certainly the road has been built recently by the Improvement Commission and I venture to say that anybody who will take the pains to look at that retaining wall will see that the timber could not have been in proper condition when iit was put in. More than that, I 3ubmit that it is not a judicious expenditure of money to build it of wood at all. I think that whatever we are doing in the way of improvement ought to be of a permanent character, something that will not require to be renewed in a few years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I will see that the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) is called to the attention of the commissioners. I am inclined to agree with him in what he has said and I shall see that it receives attention.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I went over that portion of the road with a member of the commission who pointed out to me the work that the commission had done in that particular place to prevent the sliding away of the bank into the river. It had been done by a system of drainage and not by a system of putting in timber. If I remember correctly, he said that before the commission took charge of the road, there had been some work done in the way my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) mentions, but if I am correct, he told me that they had not done work of that kind, having confined their efforts to a system of drainage which he said had been very successful, as the landslides which had occurred in the past had been almost entirely, if not altogether prevented. I think on the whole, the work of the commission has been very good.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
That is so far as
my observation goes, I do not profess to be very competent to judge. I say, however, that they have not been altogether successful in their ideas of landscape gardening. To take Strathoona park for example, I think there is too much concrete in sight there, and too many little scattered bushes instead of the system that is usually followed in landscape, gardening, of massing large clumps of shrubs together in an artistic way. Any one who happens to look at Strathcona park will see little shrubs not gathered together in clumps, but dotted all over the place, presenting what does not seem to me to be as good an appearance as it might otherwise be. I think it might be a judicious expenditure for the commission to get sometimes the services of an expert landscape gardener in doing work of that kind. So far as the structural part is concerned, the commission has so far as I know, and so far as I am able to judge done very excellent work in a very inexpensive way.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
The matter I Tefer to is this. When you go a short distance up from the grandstand at Rockcliffe where the cars stop in the early part of the season, and diverge from the old road and get onto the new driveway, you see a part that is kept from sliding away by a system of logs in line with the roadway and with cross I logs to hold them together. These logs of [DOT] decayed wood have evidently been put

there for the purpose of keeping the earth from sliding down into the river. That, I would assume was part of the driveway, and that I would assume, I do not think there is much douht about it, would be built by the Improvement Commission. I submit it was an injudicious expenditure of money. I do not propose to press that further to-night, but before leaving the subject, I would point out, as further evidence, that surmounting that retaining wall is a metal guard rail, to my mind, of a very suitable character, and all a part of the same scheme as I understand. But, unless there was very great haste required to make that connection, I do not understand the reason for making that of timber. As I have said, there is ample rock, and the tendency now is to build such constructions of concrete.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: It was only an impression on my part that another system had been adopted. It may be, as the hon. member has said, that this is the work of the commission, but I know that at some portion of that road it was pointed out to me that the prevention of landslides had been accomplished-or an attempt had been made to accomplish it-by means of a system of drainage. I remember the point to which my hon. friend refers. It would seem from his statement that it is the work of the commission.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: How much has been paid out to the Ottawa Improvement Commission? Also I would like to know whether there is a maximum amount fixed beyond which the government will not pay. Also, has the government had under consideration the creation of Ottawa into a federal district, and the disfranchisement of public servants? There is an opinion in certain parts of the country that it would be well to follow the American example and that our capital should be a federal district, and should be represented by the Prime Minister from time to time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
The sums expended by the Ottawa Improvement Commission from the beginning of their operations down to the end of last year-calendar year, I take it-were as follows:
Construction	$645,750	00Maintenance	111,181	01Other expenditures	
26*128	79Purchase of property.. ..	29,259	46

.	.	$941,049 26
