These are figures which the hon. member will find in ' Hansard ', more in detail, as I gave them at an earlier stage in answer to a question. With regard to making a federal district of Ottawa, that has Mr. LENNOX.
occasionally occupied our attention, but I am bound to say that the idea has not found general favour. There is a point of marked difference between Washington and Ottawa which adds to the difficulty of such a plan. Washington is a residential city simply, but Ottawa is and, while we have the magnificent power available near the city, must continue to be, an industrial centre, and such a city is rather unwilling to give up its franchise. The idea has occasionally engaged our attention, but it would be incorrect to say that our very grave attention has been given to it. I do not think that the citizens of Ottawa would view it with favour. However, the idea is well worth considering.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) has not stated whether there is a maximum sum up to which the government intend to pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: No, the Ottawa Commission have, from time to time, made plans of their own, but we have only approved of them so far as our appropriations would enable us to do so. The only limitation the government has fixed is that provided by the Acts hitherto passed and this resolution. If the commissioners have schemes involving the expenditure of more money, they must come to this parliament and receive approval at a later stage.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: In regard to beautifying the capital, I am sure the Prime Minister has noted some of the industrial establishments of the city belching forth a great deal of smoke and a great deal of useful fuel, which is very bad for the clothes-lines all over the city. Has he ever suggested to the Improvement Commission the advisability of having smoke consumers placed on these tall chimneys in the vicinity of the Chaudiere and elsewhere? In England, as the First Minister knows, there is no such thing as one of these chimneys to be seen in any part of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
I do not think the Ottawa Improvement Commission have control over either the tall chimneys or the clothesi-lines. With the immense power available in the Ottawa river and its tributaries, I should think its use would probably diminish the evil to which the hon. member has called attention. It should not be so serious in the future as in the past, and the clothes-lines will have a better chance.
Resolution reported, read the second time and agreed to.
Mr. FIELDING moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 230) respecting the city of Ottawa.
Motion agreed t-o, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.

speechtext: Mr. FIELDING moved that the House go into committee on certain proposed resolutions respecting bounties. He said: The Act respecting the granting of bounties on iron and steel, as respects the greater part of the bounties, that is to say: those that are paid on pig iron, puddled bars and steel ingots, will expire on the 31st of December next, and the parties interested have had ample notice, therefore, of the time when these bounties will cease to be payable. But there is one item of the steel bounties not limited in time, and that is the bounty paid on the manufacture of rods. We have thought it desirable therefore, to introduce an Act to repeal that particular bounty, but, as there has been no previous notice we propose that the bounty should cease on 1st of July, 1911, thus giving them six months notice beyond the time when the other bounties will expire.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Will the hon. minister please explain the last clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: The bounties are only payable on rods manufactured for the purpose of being manufactured into wire. All bounties cease on 30th of June except that, if they have actually made and sold rods prior to that date payment may be made after 30th of June. That is the effect of the arrangement.

Motion agreed to, and resolution was considered in committee, reported, read the second time and agreed to.
Mr. FIELDING moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 231) respecting bounties on iron and steel made in Canada.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

I do not understand why this legislation should be rushed through now. There must be something behind all this that is not disclosed. Here is a case pending in the Privy Council to decide what the rights of these people are as between the province and the Dominion. It has been decided by the Exchequer Court, decided by the Supreme Court, and leave of appeal granted the other day by the Privy Council in England where it will be decided in a few months more. Why in the world at this stage of the session is this Bill to be rushed through? It makes one very suspicious. I can't see how the public needs require any such Bill as this to be passed at this time. The Dominion government own some land out there, they do not own all the land in the railway belt, as was clearly proved on the discussion two or three days ago. They only own some land that has not been sold, and the Dominion has no right to say anything about these water-rights on land that has been alienated. Why should this Bill be pressed to make a disposition of those disputed rights while the other suit is pending? It is a strange position for tlie government to take. I am not satisfied until I hear some more reasons. There must be, according to the common expression, a nigger in the wood pile somewhere. This is not legislation that appeals to me as being at all necessary. Somebody or other wants to get an advantage of somebody else, and the government, in my opinion, is trying to help somebody to get the advantage ahead of the decision of the Privy Council. If that is an unfounded suspicion, it can be removed by a frank and clear statement of the reason of this legislation other than appears on the face of it. The government must know it. We have a right to the information without being called upon to make charges against any minister of the Crown. It is not necessary for me to say that, because I have no charge to lay, I shall not get the jnformation I am entitled to. But I suspect, and have cause to suspect, iby the character of this legislation, by the facts disclosed, by the judgment of the Exchequer Court which was read the other night, that there is some ulterior motive in this legislation, and I am not prepared without further information to vote for this Bill; on the contrary, it seems to me that we would, be justified in vigorously opposing it, even for days, if necessary. It is not quite fair to the opposition or to the people of the country for a contentious piece of legislation like this to be brought in when hon. gentlemen have begun packing their trunks, and getting ready for prorogation. This is not the way to get prorogation. This is the most contentious legislation that could be brought in involving as it does a ques-Mr. GUTHRIE.
tion of provincial rights, and trying to anticipate the decision of the courts of justice. I am bound to protest against the government arranging a day for prorogation, and then rushing in legislation of this kind, and expecting it to go through, because the members want to get home on a certain day. I am prepared to unpack my trunk and to send word to peopie with whom I have made engagements telling them that the public business requires me to stay longer rather than submit to legislation of this character. I cannot see how this government needs this legislation before next session. I have had no reason given to me why any such legislation should be brought forward at this stage of the session. It would be much more intelligent legislation if we should pass it after the Privy Council has decided what the rights of the parties are in the case that is now pending for decision. I would urge the Minister of the Interior to say if on reflection it is not a reasonable proposition that was made by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), that this legislation should stand over until next session when we would be able to consider it in a more satisfactory way, assuring the minister, as I do, that I will assist him in passing legislation which would properly deal with the question. ince of British Columbia, so that by se-grating the water from the land, the minister would simply be complicating the matter further instead of straightening it out. The purpose of the one having reference to the segregation of the water from the land is in pursuance of the policy of a conservation of the water resources of this 'country to which the whole country has given its approval, and no place more

strongly than in this parliament. That is to say, the right in the water should be hept as closely as possible under the control of the Crown and it should not pass from the Crown's control to private control except for purposes designated by and satisfactory to the Crown. In regard to the confirmation of the rights granted by the province of British Columbia, it is Conceded that this is necessary where those Tights have not already been confirmed by the Dominion. In the case of several of the large undertakings in the railway belt, "where large amounts of money were involved, the parties seemed their authority from the provincial government, and came to the Dominion government and got a, quitclaim, or a grant of the Dominion nght, but the small holders did not do that. The small holder was content with the right which he had got from the province of British Columbia, and unless we get this authority we are asking for today, the small holder will not be in the position that the large holder is in, but will be absolutely at the mercy of the pirate, whereas the large holder is protected by the quitclaim he got from the Dominion government. Now, I think it is only fair that the small holder should be put m the same position as the large holder, that what he failed to get by not coming to the Dominion government we should give him by the authority of this parliament. Then in regard to the granting of rights for the future, no man is going to invest his money in the development of water-power in the railway belt, in new enterprises, unless he gets a security of title. Now, I suppose that neither the province of British Colum-,bla' nor anybody in the Dominion wishes to hold back the development of the water resources of that railway belt for one moment. It is desirable that capital should be secured, and if it is desired to introduce capital in any enterprise at present, there is no security of title, and no secure title can be got.
Does the hon. minister say that capital would be invested in any right granted by the Dominion, when in view of the case now before the courts capitalists realize that any grant so made might be upset by_ the Privy Council, and particularly m view of the fact that two courts have already given a decision distinctly affirming the principle that the moment the land is alienated from the Dominion it comes under the jurisdiction of the province.

But, if this Bill is passed, and this government is clothed with authority to issue a grant, then an enterprise can come and get the authority of this government, and go to the province and get its quitclaim, and it would be an absolutely secure title, just as some years ago the enterprises, my hon. friend has spoken of, went to the provincial government, got their grants, and came to the Dominion, and got the grant of such rights as the Dominion was able to give. If this legislation is passed any new enterprise can be put in the same position, and development in the railway belt will not be retarded. A friend of mine who is interested in this subject has called my attention to this Bill. I have listened carefully to the discussion. If the minister's object is to obtain a confirmation of rights, then, I submit, that the language

used in section 4 is not very apt-not as lawyers usually read it. The first portion of section 4 vests in the Crown, the rights to the water ' unless and until and except only so far as some right therein, or to the use thereof, inconsistent with the right of the Crown, and which is not a public right or a right common to the public, is established.' Now, that language, especially the phrase ' is established ' is not found usually in public statutes and is not one of which we can get a ready definition in any judicial dictionary known to me or in any law relating to the interpretation of statutes. Where you have a law passed confirmatory of deeds of title, the statement that such grants at a certain time, setting them out in general language and declaring these to be confirmed, is sufficient, unless there is a desire to becloud the question. The other is entirely unnecessary for the object if the object be merely to confirm the rights regularly obtained in the past. There have been grants I understand made by the Crown under order in council. I am told that- they are in the nature of quitclaim. But, so far as I have had experience in dealing with grants from the Crown, I see nothing but quitclaims in them. The Crown never guarantees titles to any grantee, but simply gives the grantee whatever right is there, and this means nothing more in law or in fact than a quitclaim deed passing between individuals. If 'the right to grant these quitclaim deeds, to use the ordinary phraseology, has been exercised in the past, I do not see the point of my hon. friend from Yukon (Mr. Congdon) about this legislation being necessary to give the minister power to make these grants, because that power has been exercised in the past. And as a matter of policy, it would seem right that a clause should be passed confirming rights which have been regularly obtained from the authorities whom the public had a right to suppose had the power to give these in the past. The whole question as to water-powers is under appeal, leave to appeal having been obtained from the Privy Council. The Privy Council sits in July, and decision will be given before we meet again in October. The policy of parliament in the past has not been to go in and assume a right to exercise any power affecting property or civil rights while these matters were sub judice.

speechtext: There is a principle involved in this Bill that is a little strange. As it is worded ' the driver of a motor car, by giving his name or address, can escape liability both criminal and civil.' If we are going to put a statute of this kind on the statute-book, let us put it in a more sensible form than this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
subtopic: PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS. INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext: The section of the Bill as reported by the committee imposes a penalty on the motor car driver, who, with intent to escape liability, either civil or criminal, drives on without giving assistance or his name or address. Does my hon. friend think it is a hardship if a man is arrested and brought to trial in such a case?

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
subtopic: PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS. INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext: No, I do not think that at all, but I think he ought to be liable under the code for the greater offence, as this reads he would escape that liability by simply calling out a name. You are creating a confusion of legislation; you are saying that a man is liable to a fine of $50 at the most no matter how many people he might injure, and that he can escape that penalty by simply shouting out his name and address.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
subtopic: PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS. INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext: If the hon. member, (Mr. Lancaster) will look at the Criminal Code, he will find that there is a provision making a man liable for an accident. This is something in addition. I have not the Criminal Code before me, but I was on the committee, as was the member for Portage la Prairie, I think, and we discussed it very carefully with the Minister of Justice. The hon. member will find that there is a provision in the code against furious driving, and this is only an additional provision in case the driver of the car fails to stop.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
subtopic: PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS. INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext: It will become substitutional so far as motor cars are concerned. That is my pbjection to the legislation.
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
subtopic: PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS. INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext: The whole point of my hon. friend's objection, as I understand it, is that this will be a substitute for the legislation already in existence. I do not think so. That was not the intention of the committee. The intention was simply to create a new offence.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
subtopic: PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS. INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext: As I understand the object of the legislation it is this. When an accident has occurred on the highway owing to the presence of a motor car, whether there has been negligence on the part-of the persons driving the motor car or not, absolutely irrespective of that consideration, the motor car must stop and the driver must tender assistance and give his name and address. If he fails to do that,; then he is liable, on summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding $50 in costs.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
subtopic: PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS. INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
subtopic: PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS. INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext: That would be irrespective of whether he is in fault or not. If the accident occurs, and he drives on without tendering assistance or without giving his name and address, then he is liable. I think, perhaps, the wording of it might be improved a little in the last line, but apart from that it would seem to; me to have that meaning.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
subtopic: PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS. INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext: What I mean is this. Under the general Criminal Code, I do not have it here, but I think I know its effect* if any man whether he be a motor car driver or a wheel-barrow runner for that matter, or the driver of a horse, drives furiously' negligently and dangerously along the highway he is liable. But under this section, it seems to me that if a motor car driver does that he will escape the penalty imposed by simply giving his name and address, without rendering assistance to the parties he has injured. Under this section he is not required to do both, and I think he should be made to do both. I would, therefore, suggest that the word ' or ' be struck out and the word ' and ' substituted. If a man causes an accident he should not escape liability by merely-shouting out his name and address. If he is a man at all, he ought to render assistance to the injured as well as be known so that he may be sued for civil damages.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
subtopic: PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS. INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext:
I agree entirely with my hon. friend, but I suggest that the purpose might be served by inserting the word 1 without ' after the word ' or.'
Mr. LANCASTER, If you say that he should render assistance and give his name and address I would agree. As long as the driver is required to do both.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, The Bill has been carefully considered by the committee, and certainly the intention was not to substitute one .offence for another, but

simply to add an offence to the one already existing. It seems to me that intention is so obvious that I cannot understand the objection of my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster).

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
subtopic: PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS. INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext: The hon. Prime Minister may be right in saying that the intention was to create a new offence, but even if that is so, the legislation as framed will be of no practical benefit if a man can escape liability by simply shouting out his name and address without rendering assistance. I am pointing out that he ought to do both. I would move that the word ' or ' be struck out and the word ' and ' substituted.

Amendment agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speechtext: On motion that the House go into committee on Bill (No. 75) to amend the Criminal Code.-Mr. Harris.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that, as a matter of principle, this Bill is not good. A person dealing with ordinary property in the way referred to by this Bill would be, .prima facie, guilty of theft. But it is proposed here to pass a Bill for a minor punishment in this particular ease. The provision of the Bill is that if any person takes a motor car, or automobile to be used, or driven, without the consent of the owner, he is liable to a penalty. But if he were to take a mante horse or wheel-barrow he would be prima facie guilty of theft.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Prima facie only.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
Yes, unless he can show his authority. But the plea of a person that he intends to return the property, judge or jury might not conscientiously accept. But if such a thing is made to apply to motor cars, it should apply to horses, wheel-barrows, kits of tools, and other property. Why protect the owners of motor cars as against the owners of any other property? If people take motor cars without the owners' consent they should be punished. But why special legislation respecting motor cars that does not apply to other property such as I have described? We should have the same Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
legislation for all. So on principle, I am not prepared to vote for the Bill.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: This Bill was before the special committee, and its passage was urged by a number of gentlemen who said that this taking of automobiles for use without the consent of the owners requires special legislation. IMs claimed that nearly all the accidents are caused by chauffeurs, who are on what are known as ' joy rides '. Having taken the owner to his office, let us say, the chauffeur goes off without the owners consent and somebody is injured. The only argument used against this measure is that it is special legislation. But it is legislation that is needed to meet a special difficulty.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Lancaster) objects to this Bill because it is special legislation, and in favour of motor car owners. His position is amusing in view of the fact that a moment ago he supported a Bill dealing specially with motor cars. But in that case it appeared to be directed against the owner of the car. There is no legislation providing that if a man is driving a horse-drawn vehicle, and somebody is injured, he must stop and give his number and address. This Bill is necessary, because, as the hon. member for Garleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), has said, a large proportion of the accidents are due to the fact that cars are taken without the consent of the owners. It is almost im-posible to punish this offence under the existing law. In England they have found it impossible to punish a man for taking a car without the owner's consent, and have even been driven to the expedient of trying the offender for theft of the gasolene used, and they are obliged to meet the case by special legislation. It is not for the benefit of motor owners, but for the benefit of the public at large, and for this reason , I am heartily in favour of this measure.
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the Bill.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
Notwithstanding what has just been said by the hon. gentleman, I think this is legislation purely in the interest of the owners of motor cars. It does not say anything about furious driving, there is not a word about doing injury to any one else. It is idle to imagine that this is intended to 'protect people on the road; it is intended to protect the owner of the car so that it will not suffer any injury, so that the machinery may not be damaged, and he will not have to spend money to repair it. I do not agree with the hon. member for Carlton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell) that the owners of motor cars are entitled to any special legislation. The farmer with his horse in the pasture, the

livery stable keeper, with his horse in the barn, the artisan with his kit of tools, are just as much entitled to protection as the owner of a motor car. But some people who may have influence enough with the government to send agents to Ottawa to plead for special rights, have been successful with the government. I move in amendment to add the words ' or other personal property,' after the words, 'motor car.'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend will not persevere in his amendment. He will see at once the reason of this legislation. There have been occasionally parties who have stolen a ride, or stolen a horse, or a kit of tools from another workman, but the cases have been so rare that there has been no need of special legislation. But since the motor car has come into general use the daily papers are full of reports of accidents which have been caused by chauffeurs taking a car without permission of the master, or some one jumping into the car and moving it. Now the motor car is a vehicle of such a character that unless it is directed by a skilled man, accidents are likely to be numerous.
Amendment, Mr. Lancaster, negatived.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speechtext: I wish to ask the House to return to the order for the introduction of Bills, in order that I may have leave to introduce Bill (No. 232) to amend the Government Railways Act. The other day when I was putting through a measure amending the general Railway Act, I gave notice of this Bill. It transpires that we have made the government railways subject to all the liabilities of an ordinary railway as to fires, the Act has been changed to place them in the same position, but we have not put in the saving clause in reference to the $5,000 that is in the Railway Act. I merely wish to put the government railways in the same position as ordinary railways.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.	_
